intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 12 units · revolutions to annexation

This book runs from the American and French revolutions to Eritrea’s federation and annexation (1952–62). Grade 12 then starts at 1945 globally and at 1961 for the armed struggle. Keep the two years in sequence: **this file ends where Grade 12 Unit 5 begins**.
Every essay: *background → causes (long + short) → course (turning dates) → results*. A date without a “so what” is half a mark.

cards.title: 1.1 Background to the revolution
body: The United Kingdom of Great Britain came into existence in 1707, when the governments of England and Scotland were united.
The term British came to refer to both the English and the Scots.
By the 18th century trade and industry in Britain were growing, which led to an ever-increasing middle class.
The middle class favored expansion of both trade and Britain’s world empire.
In North America, Britain controlled Canada as well as 13 colonies on the eastern coast of the present United States.

cards.title: 1.2 Causes of the revolution
body: For more than 150 years, England allowed the colonies to develop politically and economically with little interference.
A series of actions by the British changed this policy and caused the American Revolution.
After the Seven Years War, British leaders wanted to get new revenues from the colonies.
In 1765, the British Parliament imposed the Stamp Act (a piece of law) on the colonies.
The act required that certain printed materials, such as legal documents and newspapers, carry a stamp showing that a tax had been paid to Britain.

cards.title: 1.3 The beginning of the revolution
body: The Second Continental Congress met in 1775 and formed an army called the Continental Army, with George Washington as commander in chief.
On July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Dependence written by Thomas Jefferson.
The Declaration of Independence was an historic political document that declared the colonies to be independent states free from the British Crown.
The American Declaration had formally begun the Revolution.
The war against Great Britain was a war between two unequal armies.

cards.title: 1.4 Foreign Support and British Defeat
body: Support from other countries played a big role in the success of American Revolution.
The French supplied arms and money to the rebels from the beginning of the war.
French officers and soldiers also served in Washington’s army.
During the Revolution, the British were faced with war against much of Europe, as well as against the Americans.
When the British army was forced to surrender to combined American and French forces under Washington in 1781, the British decided to end the war.

body: By the 1760s Britain held 13 colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America plus Canada after the Seven Years’ War. Colonists were mostly self-taxing through their assemblies. London then tried to make them pay for the empire.

tips.text: In North America Britain controlled Canada as well as 13 colonies on the eastern coast of the present United States.
The 13 colonies had gradually evolved into largely independent selfgoverning units.
After the Seven Years War, however, Britain wanted to get new revenues from the colonies and tried to interfere in the internal affairs of the colonists.
Several laws imposed by the British parliament angered the colonists and caused the American Revolution.
The colonists organized several Continental Congresses.

In July 1776, the Second Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence and set up the continental army under the command of George Washington. This formally began the American Revolution.
Though British forces were much superior to the American revolutionaries, the colonists won the war with substantial help from other countries.
In the Treaty of Paris that ended the war, Britain formally recognized American independence.
By 1789 a United States of America had a new constitution based on a federal system and separation of powers.

cards.title: 2.1 The cause of French revolution
body: The causes of the French Revolution include both long-term problems and immediate events.
The long-term causes are to be found in the unjust foundations of French society.
The Revolution was also influenced by the Enlightenment and the success of the American Revolution.
The slogan of the Revolution – Liberty, Equality, Fraternity – reflected the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers.
The immediate cause of the Revolution was the crisis in the economy.

cards.title: 2.2 Course of the revolution
body: The Estates-General was composed of representatives from the three Estates of French society.
The First and Second Estates had about three hundred delegates each.
The Third Estate had almost six hundred delegates.
To fix France’s financial problems, most members of the Third Estate wanted to set up a constitutional government that would abolish the tax exemptions of the clergy and nobility.
In the beginning of the meeting members of the Third Estate demanded reform in the voting system of the Estate-General.

cards.title: French Revolution
body: France was an absolute monarchy with a society of orders: clergy, nobility, everyone else (the Third Estate) paying most of the tax. War debt (including aid to America) plus bad harvests broke the treasury.

1789: Estates-General → National Assembly → Bastille → Declaration of the Rights of Man. The king is forced to Paris. Church land is sold. Constitution of 1791 tries a limited monarchy, then war and fear produce the Republic, the Terror, and the Directory. Napoleon ends the chaos, exports some reforms, then falls (1815 Waterloo). Congress of Vienna tries to put kings back; the ideas do not die.

Phases to keep straight: 1789 moderate / constitutional; 1792 republic and war; 1793–94 Terror (Committee of Public Safety); Directory; 1799 Napoleon as consul then emperor; 1815 defeat and Vienna. Napoleon’s Code, metric-ish modern admin, and the shock of occupation spread nationalism in Germany and Spain — an unintended result.

glossary.meaning: Nationalism is the unique cultural identity of a people based on common language, religion, and national symbols.

tips.text: The nature of the social and political order in France was the fundamental cause of the Revolution.
The deteriorating economy as the result of financial mismanagement, on the other hand, served as an immediate cause to the beginning of the revolution.
To raise taxes the King was forced to call on the ancient assembly of three estates representing all the classes in France.
Disagreement over the voting system resulted in the breakaway of the representatives of the third estate, which was the only taxpaying estate.
The representatives of the third estate called themselves the national assembly and chose to declare the body sovereign as it represented the vast majority of the people of France.
The storming of the Bastille prison in Paris on the 14th of July is regarded as being the landmark event that led to the beginning of the revolution.
Inspired by the storming of the Bastille, the people in the cities and the countryside revolted against the ancient regime.
On August 26, 1789 the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen.

In the events that followed the National Assembly framed a Constitution which could restore social order, but differences within the Assembly over whether to retain the monarchy or abolish it led to further disorders.
Meanwhile, the Assembly declared war against Austria and Prussia due to the hostile stance against France.

cards.title: Industrialisation and nationalism
body: Industry starts in Britain: coal, iron, steam, textile machines, capital, empire markets, agricultural surplus, relatively stable politics. Factories pull people into towns. New class split: industrial owners and a wage-working class. Later the same kit spreads to Belgium, France, Germany, the USA.
**Social impact:** longer paid work, child labour, slums, but also cheaper cloth, new transport, unions, socialist ideas, public health fights.

**Nationalism:** the idea that people who share language/history should have a state. It unifies Germany and Italy; it also threatens multi-national empires (Austria-Hungary, Ottoman). Combined with industry it gives Europe the guns and the motive for empire — which is Part 2.

Why Britain first — list at least four on the paper: coal and iron close together, navigable rivers/ports, already commercial farming, colonies as markets and cotton source, inventors plus capital, a state that mostly allowed private enterprise. Social question the book wants: who gained cheap goods and who paid in slums and 14-hour days?

cards.title: 3.1.1 The Spread of Industrialization
body: By the mid-19th century, Great Britain had become the world’s first and richest industrial nation.
The Industrial Revolution spread to the rest of Europe at different times and speeds.
First to be industrialized in continental Europe were Belgium, France, and the German states.
In these places, governments were very active in encouraging the development of industrialization.

cards.title: 3.1.2 The Social Impact of Industrialization
body: The Industrial Revolution considerably changed the social life of Europe and the world.
The two new classes were the industrial middle class and the industrial working class.
In 1750, the population of Europe was estimated at 140 million.
By 1850, the population had almost doubled to 266 million.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Background
body: After the defeat of Napoleon, European rulers wanted to restore the old order, which existed before Napoleon.
In order to achieve their goal the great powers (Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia) met at the Congress of Vienna in September 1814 to arrange a final peace settlement.
The leader of the Congress was the Austrian foreign minister, Prince Klemens von Metternich.
Metternich advocated that lawful monarchs from the royal families that had ruled before Napoleon should be restored to their positions of power in order to keep peace and stability in Europe.

cards.title: 3.2.2 The Revolutions
body: Despite Liberal and Nationalist successes in France and Belgium, the Conservative order still dominated much of Europe in the middle of the 19th century.
Revolution in France was again the cause for revolution in other countries.
Severe economic problems beginning in 1846 brought problems in France to the lower middle class, workers, and peasants.
At the same time, members of the middle class demanded for the right to vote.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Breakdown of the Concert of Europe
body: The revolutions of 1848 had largely failed.
The Concert of Europe also failed with the start of the Crimean War.
The Crimean War was the result of a long-standing struggle between Russia and the Ottoman Empire.
The Ottoman Empire had controlled much of the Balkans in southeastern Europe for centuries.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Italian Unification
body: The royal house of Savoy ruled the Kingdom of Piedmont, which included Piedmont, the island of Sardinia, Nice, and Savoy.
The Kingdom of Piedmont was the strongest Italian state.
The ruler of the kingdom, beginning in 1849, was King Vittorio Emmanuel II.
Cavour was a brilliant political leader.

cards.title: 3.3.3 German Unification
body: After the failure of the Frankfurt Assembly to achieve German unification in 1848 and 1849, Prussia became the leader of the German aspiration for unification.
In the course of the nineteenth century, Prussia had become a strong and prosperous state.
The Prussian king had firm control over both the government and the army.
Prussia was also known for its militarism or reliance on military strength.

lessons.title: Europe and North America from 1850 to 1914

cards.title: 3.4.1 Europe
body: In 1832, Parliament issued a law that increased the number of male voters.
In the 1850s and 1860s, Parliament continued to make both social and political reforms that helped the country to remain stable.
By 1871, Great Britain had a two-party parliamentary system.
For the next 50 years, these two parties (the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party) were in and out of power.

cards.title: 3.4.2 North America
body: Two factions fought about the division of power in the new government.
The Federalists favored a strong central government.
The Republicans, fearing central power, wanted the federal government to be subordinate to the state governments.
By the mid-19th century, the issue of American national unity had reemerged.

cards.title: 3.4.3 The Working Classes movement
body: The desire to improve their working and living conditions led many industrial workers to form Socialist political parties and trade unions.
In 1848, The Communist Manifesto was published.
Marx believed that all of world history was a history of class struggles.
One class of people owned the means of production (land, raw materials, money) and thus had the power to control government and society.

cards.title: 3.4.4 International Rivalries
body: At the same time, Bismarck maintained a separate treaty with Russia and tried to remain on good terms with Great Britain.
In 1890, Emperor William II dismissed Bismarck from power and took control of Germany’s foreign policy.
The emperor changed Bismarck’s foreign policy.
One of the changes he made in Bismarck’s foreign policy was to the treaty with Russia.

lessons.title: Western Society, Culture and Science Between 1850-1914

cards.title: 3.5.1 Society
body: In Europe, by the end of the 19th century more and more people lived in cities.
By 1890, urban dwellers had increased to 60 percent in England, 25 percent in France, 30 percent in Prussia, and 10 percent in Russia.
Urban populations grew quickly because of the vast migration to cities from rural areas.
In cities, people found jobs in factories and, later, in the service sectors and the professions.

cards.title: 3.5.2 Science and Scientific Ideas
body: The Scientific Revolution created a rational approach to the study of the natural world.
The Industrial Revolution increased interest in scientific research.
By the 1830s, new discoveries in science had led to many practical benefits that affected all Europeans.
Science started to have greater impact on people.

cards.title: 3.5.3 Cultural developments
body: At the end of the 18th century, a new intellectual movement, known as Romanticism, emerged as a reaction to the ideas of the Enlightenment.
The Enlightenment stressed reason as the chief means for discovering truth.
The romantics emphasized feelings, emotion, and imagination as sources of knowledge.
The Romantics believed that emotion and sentiment were only understandable to the person experiencing them.

glossary.meaning: Socialism is a system in which society, usually in the form of the state, owns and controls the main means of production, such as factories and utilities.

tips.text: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain during the last half of the 18th century and spread to the rest of Europe at different times and speeds in the following century.
An Industrial Revolution also occurred in the new nation, the United States.
Apart from changing the mode of production and products, the Industrial Revolution considerably changed the social life of Europe and the world.
This change was evident in the first half of the 19th century in the growth of cities and the emergence of two new social classes.
The two new classes were the industrial middle class and the industrial working class.

At the beginning the conditions of the industrial working class was very poor. These difficult working and living conditions created by the industrial Revolution gave rise to a movement known as socialism.
Socialism is a system in which society, usually in the form of the government, owns and controls the basic means of production, such as factories and utilities.
After the defeat of Napoleon, European rulers wanted to restore the old order that existed before Napoleon.

In order to achieve their goal, the great powers of Europe met at the Congress of Vienna. These rulers were Conservatives who wanted to keep the status qou. They were also against revolutions and radical changes.
In contrast to this Conservative order the forces of Liberalism and Nationalism demanded political change. These forces continued to grow and finally brought about the revolutions of 1848.

cards.title: 4.1 Colonialism in Southeast Asia
body: Southeast Asia is a region in Asia comprised of Indochina, the Malay Peninsula, and the Malay Archipelago.
The region is bordered on the north by China; on the east by the Pacific Ocean; on the south by the Indian Ocean; and on the west by the Indian Ocean, the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh, and India.
Today there are eleven countries in Southeast Asia: Brunei, Cambodia, East Timor, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar (formerly Burma), the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
Unit-Four Colonial rule and influence in Asia In 1800 in this region, only two areas (the Spanish Philippines and the Dutch East Indies) were ruled by Europeans.
By 1900, however, almost the whole region was under Western rule.

cards.title: 4.2 British colonialism in India
body: Over the course of the 18th century, British power in India had increased while the power of the Mogul rulers had declined.
A trading company, the British East India Company, was given power by the British government to become actively involved in India’s political and military affairs.
In 1857, a growing Indian opposition to the British led to a revolt.
The revolt was known by the British as the Great Rebellion or the Sepoy Mutiny, but, Indians call it the First War of Independence.
The revolt started when the British arrested some sepoys.

cards.title: 4.3 China under European influence
body: In 1800, after a long period of peace and prosperity, the Qing dynasty of the Manchus was at the height of its power.
In the beginning of the 20th century, however, the Qing dynasty collapsed.
The main reason for the rapid decline and fall of the Qing dynasty was the external pressure applied to Chinese society by Western countries.
Population growth created food shortage and frequent famine.
By 1800, Europeans had been in contact with China for more than two hundred years.

cards.title: 4.4 The rise of modern Japan
body: By the mid of the 19th century, Western nations began to approach Japan in the hope of opening the country to foreign economic activities.
The first foreign power to succeed with Japan was the United States.
In the summer of 1853, an American fleet of four warships arrived in Edo Bay (now Tokyo Bay).
Later, Japan agreed to the Treaty of Kanagawa.
In 1858, the U.S. consul signed a more detailed treaty.

cards.title: Empire
body: Industrial states want raw materials, markets, coaling stations and prestige. The “new imperialism” after ~1870 is faster and more territorial than older trading posts.

cards.title: Asia
body: **India:** Company rule → 1857 uprising → Crown Raj. Britain takes revenue, builds rails for extraction, uses Indian troops abroad. Modern politics (Congress) grows inside that cage.
**Southeast Asia:** Dutch East Indies, British Burma/Malaya, French Indochina — plantation and mineral colonies.
**China:** not fully partitioned but “carved” into spheres after the Opium Wars; unequal treaties, ports, missionaries. Reform and then revolution (1911) try to recover sovereignty.
**Japan:** Meiji modernisation — copy Western industry and army in order *not* to be colonised; then Japan becomes an imperial power itself (Korea, later China).

tips.text: Southeast Asia is a region in Asia comprising of Indochina, the Malay Peninsula, and the Malay Archipelago.
The process of colonization in this region began with Great Britain.
The British controlled Singapore, Burma and Malaya (modern day Malaysia).

France took over Vietnam and Cambodia in the 1880s; during the following decade, France completed her Indochinese empire with the annexation of Laos, leaving the kingdom of Siam (now Thailand) an independent state as a neutral buffer between British and French-ruled lands.
In 1898, during the Spanish-American War, United States naval forces defeated the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay.
After its victory, America kept the Philippines as an American colony.

Western powers governed their new colonial empires through indirect or direct rule. Their chief goals were to exploit the natural resources of these lands and to use them as markets for their own manufactured goods.
In Southeast Asia the colonized people had resisted European domination.
The resistance was manifested in the form of resistance offered by the pre-colonial rulers, peasant revolts and later by western educated nationalists.

units.title: Colonialism and Independence Movements in Latin America

cards.title: 5.1 Colonialism in Latin America
body: In the 16th century, Portugal came to dominate Brazil.
At the same time, Spain established a vast colonial empire in the Americas that included parts of North America, the whole of Central America, and most of South America.
Portuguese and Spanish possessions in the Americas were colonial empires that lasted for over three hundred years.

cards.title: 5.2 Independence Movement
body: By the end of the 18th century, the new political ideals coming from the successful revolution in North America were beginning to influence Latin America.
Social classes based on privilege divided colonial Latin America.
Peninsulares were Spanish and Portuguese officials who resided temporarily in Latin America for political and economic benefits and then returned to their mother countries.
Creoles controlled land and business but were regarded as second-class citizens by peninsulares.
Creoles were descendants of Europeans born in Latin America who lived there permanently.

cards.title: Latin America
body: Spain and Portugal held the mainland for centuries. Early 1800s: Creole elites, inspired by Enlightenment and by Spain’s collapse under Napoleon, fight independence (Bolívar, San Martín, Brazil’s different monarchic path). After independence: political instability, caudillos, export economies still tied to Britain/USA, land inequality. Formal flags, informal economic dependence.

cards.title: 5.3 Post Independence Development
body: The wars for independence had resulted in many losses of people, property, and livestock.
Poor roads, a lack of railroads, and mountains made communication, transportation, and national unity difficult.
During the course of the 19th century, the new Latin American nations would become economically dependent on Western nations.
Most of the new nations of Latin America began with republican governments, but they had had no experience in ruling themselves.
Soon after independence, strong leaders known as caudillos came to power.

tips.text: Spanish and Portuguese colonies in the Americas were colonial empires that lasted over three hundred years.
During the colonial period the intermarriage between the Native Americans and Europeans resulted to a mixed yet highly stratified society.
Spain and Portugal profited from the colonies through exploiting gold, silver, plantation and trade.
By the end of the 18th century, the new political ideals coming from the successful revolution in North America were beginning to influence Latin America.

The creole (descendants of Europeans born in Latin America who lived there permanently) were especially influenced by revolutionary ideals of equality and freedom. Thus, the creole elites began to oppose the rule of the Spanish and Portuguese.
When Napoleon overthrew the monarchies of Spain and Portugal, the authority of the Spaniards and Portuguese in their colonial empires was considerably weakened.
Using this opportunity, a series of successful revolts broke out between 1807 and 1825, and enabled most of Latin America to become independent.
Between 1830 and 1870 the new Latin American nations faced political and economic problems.

Unit-Five Colonialism and Independence Movements in Latin America building a strong state, reducing inequalities and developing a sense of national unity. Besides, the new Latin American nations found themselves economically dependent on Western nations.
The U.S. in particular was increasingly involved in the affairs of the Latin American countries.

cards.title: 6.1 The Scramble for Africa
body: Before 1880, Europeans controlled only a small part of the African continent directly.
Between 1880 and 1900, however, because of rivalries among European powers, Great Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Italy, Spain, and Portugal placed almost all of Africa under European rule.
The process by which Africa came under European colonial powers is known as the Scramble for Africa.
By 1808, both Great Britain and the United States had made the slave trade illegal.
Other European countries eventually did the same.

cards.title: 6.2 Colonial Rule in Africa
body: Only Liberia, which had been created as a homeland for freed United States slaves, and Ethiopia remained independent states.
Native peoples who tried to resist were crushed by the superior military force of the Europeans.
As in Southeast Asia, most European governments ruled their new territories directly or indirectly.
Indirect rule meant relying on existing political rulers and institutions.
The British especially followed this approach.

cards.title: Scramble for Africa
body: Until the late 19th century Europe held coastal footholds. Then explorers, missionaries, companies and rival governments rush inland. Berlin Conference (1884–85) sets rules among Europeans, not Africans: claim + “effective occupation.”

By 1914 almost the whole map is coloured except Ethiopia (and Liberia). Italy later takes Libya and, after Adwa 1896 failure, seizes Eritrea earlier as a Red Sea colony (1880s–90s) — that is the local end of this unit.

Colonial rule styles: direct (often French), indirect (often British chiefs), settler (Kenya, Algeria, southern Africa), company then state. Economy: cash crops, mines, forced labour, hut tax that pushes people into wage work. Resistance is constant — military at first, then political associations.

cards.title: Africa hook
body: Explore → claim at Berlin → occupy → tax and cash crop → resist. Eritrea is Italy’s Red Sea foothold in that same scramble.

cards.title: Big spine to recite

tips.text: The Scramble for Africa was the period between the 1880s and the beginning of the First World War.

It was mainly related with the emergence of trade of goods in place of the Atlantic Slave Trade, European merchants had been increasingly interested in gaining control over the trading system of the African interior.

The main European countries that were engaged in the Scramble were Britain, France, Germany, and Belgium. However, after the Berlin Conference many European countries became involved in colonization. As a result, there was a race to occupy African territories.
The occupation of Egypt by Britain and the Congo by King Leopard of Belgium were the first major moves in what came to be the Scramble for African territories.
In 1884 Bismarck convened a conference in Berlin and invited the leading European states to discuss their conflicting interests in Africa.

The conference came up with an agreement that the area along the Congo River was to be administered by King Leopold II of Belgium as a neutral area known as the Congo Free State, in which trade and navigation were to be free.
The most important article of the General Act of Berlin Conference was Art. 34.
This article provided European colonial powers with the right to take their share in Africa, but with the required notification to the Berlin Office so as to avoid conflict among themselves.
Before the 1880s a limited number of coastal territories and African countries had been occupied by European colonizers.

By the 1914, however, with the only exception of Liberia and Ethiopia, the whole of Africa had been partitioned and occupied by the imperial powers of France, Britain, Germany, Portugal, Belgium, Spain, and Italy, and a colonial system was established.

units.title: The First World War
units.intro:
**Long causes:** alliance blocs (Triple Alliance vs Triple Entente), arms race, imperial rivalry, nationalism in the Balkans. **Spark:** Sarajevo 1914, Austria vs Serbia, alliance machinery pulls Germany, Russia, France, Britain in.

**Course:** Schlieffen plan fails; Western Front trenches; Eastern Front more mobile; war at sea and in colonies; 1917 USA in, Russia out (revolution). 1918 German spring then collapse. Armistice 11 Nov 1918.

lessons.title: Causes of the First World War

cards.title: 7.1 Causes of the First World War
body: Yet there were many more fundamental and long term causes that led European countries to war.
Unit-Seven First World War (1914-1918) A.
In the first half of the 19th century, many people believed that European states would work together and create a peaceful Europe.
Instead, European states began to compete against each other.
At the same time, Europe was divided into two opposing alliances.

cards.title: MAIN
body: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism — then a Balkan spark.

lessons.title: Courses of the First World War

cards.title: 7.2 Courses of the First World War
body: Europeans greeted the beginning of the First World War with excitement.
Government propaganda created a heightened sense of national feelings and many people were convinced that their countries were right.
The First World War was fought, almost, all over the world.
Germany had a plan to enter into northern France through Belgium.
The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front.

cards.title: 7.3 The Russian Revolution
body: Russia was not prepared militarily and technologically for the war.
Because of these reasons, Russia suffered incredible losses in the war.
Between 1914 and 1916, two million Russian soldiers were killed, and another four to six million soldiers wounded or captured.
All these factors reduced Russians’ will to continue to fight in the First World War.
Czar Nicholas II was a suppressive ruler.

cards.title: The Russian Revolution
body: **Russian Revolution:** war misery + Tsarist failure → Feb/March 1917 liberal-ish stage → Oct/Nov Bolsheviks. Russia leaves the war (Brest-Litovsk), becomes the first communist state — a Unit 8 and Grade 12 problem.

cards.title: 7.4 The End of WWI
body: The year 1917 was not a good one for the Allies.
Allied offensives on the Western Front failed and Russia withdrew from the war after the November 1917 revolution.
For Germany, the withdrawal of Russia from the war was good news.
In March 1918, Germany launched a massive attack on the Western Front.
By April, German forces were within about 80kms of Paris.

cards.title: The End of WWI
body: **Peace:** Versailles and other treaties punish Germany (blame, reparations, lost land, tiny army), redraw Eastern Europe, create League of Nations, mandate ex-Ottoman and German colonies. Many people feel cheated — fuel for Unit 8–10.

cards.title: 7.5 Impact of WWI
body: As WWI continued, it became a total war, involving a complete mobilization of resources and people.
The war forced the warring countries to organize masses of soldiers and prepare supplies for years of combat.
Germany alone, for example, had 5.5 million soldiers.
At the end of the war, vast tracts of once productive land lay in ruins, and the populations of cities such as Berlin and Vienna were at the edge of starvation.
On top of all these, Europe was hard hit by flu, which killed more people than the war did.

glossary.meaning: Mobilization is the process of assembling troops and supplies and making them ready for war.

tips.text: The First World War began after the heir to the Austrian throne, Archduke Francis Ferdinand, was assassinated by a Serbian teenager on June 28, 1914.

Though the assassination of Archduke Ferdinand was the immediate cause of the war, there were also more fundamental and long term causes to it such as extreme nationalism, hostile alliances and militarism.
The First World War was fought between two hostile groups: the Allies and the Central Powers.
At the beginning of the war, the Allies included Serbia, Russia, Britain, and France.
The Central Powers, on the other hand, included Austria-Hungary and Germany.
Later, however, Italy, Japan, China, and USA joined the Allies; whereas, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers.
After the war started, European countries mobilized their entire populations.
Close to 70 million men were conscripted to fight the war. Moreover, the war was made more deadly by the invention of new weapons such as tanks, machine guns, gases, and submarines.
Though the war was fought all over the world, the main battles were fought in Europe.
The war in Europe was fought on two fronts: the Western and Eastern Fronts.

cards.title: 8.1 Efforts for Peace and Security
body: The peace settlement at the end of World War I had sought to bring peace among the warring states.
From the beginning, however, the peace settlement left many states unhappy.
Unit-Eight Europe and USA in the Interwar Period about the Treaty of Versailles and vowed to revise it.
The League of Nations was supposed to guarantee peace and security.
One of the weaknesses of the League was the absence of the United States.

cards.title: 8.2 The Great Depression
body: At the end of 1920s and throughout 1930s, the economies of Western countries collapsed.
The Great Depression had big negative consequences on the social, economic, and political conditions of western countries.
The fundamental cause of the depression can be found in the inherent problems of capitalist economic system.
Uneven distribution of wealth and the unregulated free market are two of the main problems.
One factor was a series of economic decline in many western countries in the second half of the 1920s.

cards.title: The Great Depression
body: **Great Depression (1929–):** US crash → world trade dies → unemployment → people listen to men who promise order and revenge.

lessons.title: Interwar Political Developments in Europe and

cards.title: 8.3 Interwar Political Developments in Europe and
body: Just after the end of WWI, most European countries had democratic governments.
In a number of European countries, women were allowed to vote.
Four years of total war and four years of postwar turmoil made a return to normalcy very difficult.
A German democratic state known as the Weimar Republic was then created in its place.
The Weimar Republic faced many problems from the beginning.

cards.title: 8.4 The Rise of Dictatorial Regimes
body: In the 1920s, many European countries were parliamentarian democracies.
A dictatorial or totalitarian government is a government that tries to control the political, economic, social, intellectual, and cultural lives of its citizens.
Totalitarian governments have many characteristics in common.
Prices had risen, unemployment grew and angry workers staged series of strikes.
Italian socialists thought of staging a revolution.

cards.title: The Rise of Dictatorial Regimes
body: **Dictatorships:** Mussolini’s Italy, Stalin’s USSR (different ideology, same one-party violence), Hitler’s Germany after 1933. Japan’s military also sidelines party politics. Common tools: secret police, propaganda, youth groups, crushing unions and parliaments.

lessons.title: Cultural Developments of the Interwar Period

cards.title: 8.5 Cultural Developments of the Interwar Period
body: After the end of WWI, many interesting cultural developments emerged in Europe.
Mass Culture: Radio and Movies Some of the most important technological innovations that influenced the post First World War cultural developments were the invention of radios and movie cameras.
Radio was invented by an Italian electrical engineer, Guglielmo Marconi, at the end of the 19th century.
At the same time, Radios were produced in abundance.
Shortly before WWI, full length movies began to emerge.

cards.title: Interwar years
body: **Peace machinery:** League of Nations — no US membership, no army of its own, unanimity culture. Works on small disputes; fails when big powers cheat.

glossary.meaning: A depression is a period of low economic activity and rising unemployment.

tips.text: The peace settlements signed at the end of WWI aimed at bringing peace and security.
The League of Nations was established to guarantee this. But, many states viewed the peace settlements as unfair and were not satisfied with them.
Eastern Europe was beset by border disputes created by the peace settlements and Germany felt bitter about the Treaty of Versailles and vowed to revoke it.
Besides, the League of Nations failed to fulfill its tasks because of the absence of the US and other important actors in the organization and the League’s lack of power to enforce its principles.
The interwar period in Europe and America was marked by severe economic problems.
In 1923, hyperinflation devastated the German economy.
Europe’s economy showed some signs of recovery from 1924 to 1929 largely due to massive US loans and investments.
As Europe’s economy recovered, the relationship among European countries improved. But the economic recovery was short-lived.
In 1929, the Great Depression devastated the American and European economies.

The depression was mainly caused by a collapse in the US stock market. As a result of the crisis created by the depression, millions of Europeans and Americans were made unemployed, public morale sagged, and extreme political parties became popular.

units.intro:

lessons.title: The End of Italian Colonial Rule in Eritrea

cards.title: 11.1 The End of Italian Colonial Rule in Eritrea
body: Right from the next day, British airplanes began to fly over Eritrea, dropping leaflets promising the Eritrean people independence.
On the contrary, Britain had only 4500 soldiers, similar number of the Sudan Defence Forces, and only 20 warplanes in the Sudan.
The Italians warplanes could easily attack British targets in the Sudan, Egypt and the Middle East from their base in Eritrea.
What’s more, the Italian troops could launch a land attack against the British in the Sudan from Eritrea.
Italian attack and occupation of Sudan would endanger the Allies war effort in the Red Sea, the Middle East, and the Far East.

cards.title: 11.2 British Military Administration
body: At the same time, Britain introduced the Sudan Defense Force in Eritrea as the chief enforcers of law and order.
Instead, they decided to maintain the Italian Fascist administration in Eritrea.
Italians were kept in their offices and their land and property holdings were strengthened.
What’s more, the British Military Administration gave Italians priority over Eritreans with regard to applications for business licenses.
Land and civil disputes between Eritreans and Italians continued to be seen before Italian judges who applied the Italian fascist laws.

lessons.title: Plans of regional and International Powers over Eritrea (1941- 1945)

cards.title: 11.3 Plans of regional and International Powers over Eritrea (1941- 1945)
body: Despite the British refusal, however, Ethiopia began to actively work to realize its dream of annexing Eritrea.
The Egyptian argument was similar to those of Ethiopia.
In the memorandum it presented to the Paris Peace Conference in 1946, Egypt claimed Eritrea on the basis of historical and economic ties.
British overall strategy was, therefore, to maintain its dominance and control in this region.

As part of this strategy, the British had a plan of creating a Greater Somalia that would include British Somaliland, the former Italian Somaliland, the Ogaden (a Somali region in Ethiopia), and some parts of Kenya.

lessons.title: The End of WWII and the Subsequent Economic and Political Situations in Eritrea

cards.title: 11.4 The End of WWII and the Subsequent Economic and Political Situations in Eritrea
body: Unemployment increased, prices rose, food supplies decreased, and an acute shortage of housing appeared.
Local Eritrean industries and factories produced soap, beer, match, paper, clothes, oil, and other products.

What’s more, the British Military Administration began to systematically dismantle industries, port and airport facilities and transport networks built during the Italian period and along the course of WWII.
The British action of destroying the Eritrean economy was related with their long-term objective.
To justify their plan, the British argued that Eritrea was economically nonviable and thus could not stand as an independent country.

cards.title: 11.5 Establishment of Political Parties
body: Until October 1946, the British Military Administration prohibited the formation of political parties in Eritrea.
After Wa’ela Biet Giorgis failed, Eritreans began to form different political parties.
Generally speaking, these parties were divided into two groups: those that supported Eritrean independence and those that supported union with Ethiopia.
Al Rabita Al Islamiya (Muslim League) The first political party to be founded was the Muslim League, which was established in December 1946 in Keren, one month after Wa’ela Biet Giorgis.
The main objective of the party was unconditional and direct independence of Eritrea.

lessons.title: TheFour Great Powers and the UN over the Future of Eritrea

cards.title: 11.6 TheFour Great Powers and the UN over the Future of Eritrea
body: The Allied powers, also known as the Four Great Powers, held discussions about the former Italian colonies in Potsdam (Germany), London, and Paris.
Britain had a plan to partition Eritrea into two, give the western lowlands to the Sudan and annex the highlands and the coastal areas to Ethiopia.
In Libya, its plan was to divide the country into two and give Tripolitania to Italy and take Cyrenaica for itself.
The British plan, however, was unacceptable with other Allied members, particularly France.
France wanted the return of the colonies to Italy in the form of trusteeship.

cards.title: British period
body: 1941: British (with Allied and local fighters) end Italian rule. **British Military Administration** runs Eritrea as occupied enemy territory, not as a promised independent state. War factories and some infrastructure wind down; many Italians stay for a time; politics wakes up — union with Ethiopia vs independence vs partition talk.

The future is argued at the UN and among regional powers. Four-power talks fail to agree. The UN sends a commission. Outcomes on the table: independence, partition, union, or federation with Ethiopia. Strategic Red Sea thinking (Unit 6 geography again) sits in every capital’s file.

tips.text: In April 1941, the British took over Eritrea from the Italians. They declared Eritrea as an “Occupied Enemy Territory” and set up a military administration.
Right from the beginning of the AngloItalian war on Eritrea, the British had promised Eritreans the right to self-determination. But the British didn’t keep their promises.
After they occupied Eritrea, they did nothing to improve the economic and political lives of Eritreans.

Instead, they maintained the Italian fascist administrative and judiciary systems, and gave Italians preferential treatment in regard to jobs and other economic benefits. Thus, the hope that the British would bring peace and prosperity to Eritreans was dashed.
Worried about the prevailing economic and political situation, some prominent Eritreans established Mahber Feqri Hager in May 1941.
The main objective of the association was to present public grievances to the BMA.
At the beginning, Mahber Feqri Hager had no political objectives.

Unit-Eleven Eritrea During the British Period into two political groupings. Some members, who were supported by Ethiopia, began to agitate for the union of Eritrea with Ethiopia. These members eventually formed the Unionist Party.
Other members of Mahber Feqri Hager, such as Weldeab Weldemariam and Ibrahim Sultan established Ertra N’Ertrawyan, the sole aim of which was independence.

Between 1943 and 1945, the Allies used Eritrea as a base for their war efforts in the Middle East and North Africa. As a result, the Eritrean economy recovered. But, after WWII ended in 1945, the wartime economic boom stopped.

cards.title: 12.1 The Eritrean Constitution
body: On 14 December, 1950, the UN General Assembly elected a Bolivian diplomat, Eduardo Anze Matienzo to become a UN Commissioner in Eritrea.
Soon thereafter, he started to prepare a draft constitution in consultation with Eritrean notables and representatives of political parties.
In March 1952, an election for a Constituent Assembly was conducted.
The responsibility of the Constituent Assembly was to debate and ratify the draft constitution prepared by Anze Matienzo.
In the election, 68 people (all males) were elected to the Assembly.

body: Accordingly, it had the mandate of only ratifying the Eritrean constitution and had to dissolve after it completed its job.

The first three years of the Eritrean government was characterized by economic decline and violation of democratic rights of Eritreans by the Ethiopian government.

body: According to the provisions of the Federal Act, a Federal Council was supposed to be formed with equal number of Ethiopian and Eritrean representatives.
The task of the Federal Council was to advice Emperor Haileselasie on common matters of the Federation such as defense, foreign affairs, and currency.
Unit-Twelve From Federation to Annexation (1952-1962) The Ethiopian representative, Andargachew Messay, continuously interfered in Eritrea’s internal affairs.
In 1955, Ethiopia forced Tedla Bairu and Ali Radai to step down and replaced them with Asfa Woldemichael and Idris Mohammed Adem, respectively.
The new government of Asfeha Woldemichael banned all political parties except the Unionist party led by the pro-Ethiopia cleric Demetros Ghebremariam.

body: On 13 November 1962, Ethiopian troops stationed in Eritrea were ordered to take up positions at the main points of Asmara and other Eritrean towns.
Ethiopian jets flew over Eritrea’s main towns to intimidate the people.
Members of the Eritrean Assembly who opposed Ethiopia’s violation of the Federation were intimidated and forced to resign.
The Assembly building was surrounded by soldiers armed with machineguns.
Asfa Woldemichael accompanied by Tedla Okbit (Chief of the Eritrean Police) came to the meeting and read an Amharic statement announcing the dissolution of the federation.

tips.text: In December 1950, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 390A (V) under strong US pressure.
According to the provisions of the Resolution, the General Assembly appointed Anze Matienzo as a UN Commissioner for Eritrea.
Anze Matienzo prepared a draft constitution and supervised the election of a Constituent Assembly in 1952.
From March to July 1952, the Eritrean Constituent Assembly debated on the draft constitution prepared by Matienzo.
On July 10, 1952, the Eritrean Assembly ratified a relatively progressive constitution.
In September 1952, Ethiopia ratified the Eritrean Constitution and four days later federation became effective.
What’s more, the Eritrean Assembly elected Tedla Bairu as chief executive and Ali Radai as chairman of the Assembly.
Ethiopia viewed the federation as a temporary arrangement to be abolished gradually. Therefore, soon after the federation came into effect, it began to systematically dismantle it.
In 1953, Ethiopia abolished the Federal Council.
In 1954, it closed down the Voice of Eritrea and jailed its editors.
